title: Remainder and exponentiation
recap: The remainder operator % returns the remainder after integer division. It is useful for periodic wrapping and divisibility tests, and its operands must have integral types.

C++ has no exponentiation operator: ^ is bitwise XOR. std::pow from <cmath> performs exponentiation and returns a floating-point result, while direct multiplication can be preferable for small integer powers.
objectives: Use remainder to wrap an offset into a fixed cycle.
Use remainder to test whether an integer is even.
Call std::pow rather than mistaking ^ for exponentiation.
Print results calculated from named operands.
warnings: The % operator is for integral operands, not floating-point remainder calculations.
The ^ operator does not raise a number to a power in C++.
std::pow returns a floating-point value even when supplied integral values.
challenge: Advance weekday index 5 by 4 days and wrap it into the 0-through-6 range with %. Test whether a shipment count of 18 is even using remainder. Finally calculate 2 raised to 5 with std::pow. Keep the run deterministic and print all three results.
hints: Use (startDay + dayOffset) % daysPerWeek to wrap the index.
An integer is even when its remainder after division by 2 equals zero.
Include <cmath> and call std::pow(base, exponent); use std::boolalpha for the boolean line.
